transfer_provisions.note: Title I (priorities and allocations) functions go to the ODM Director, who redelegates them; EO 10161 had held them, and EO 10324 (definitions of solid fuels and domestic transportation) and EO 10359 (plant fibers) amended that text. Secs. 601(e) and 601(k) of EO 10480 re-prescribe the two definitions EO 10324 had amended.

effective_date_reading: The held Federal Register text of the order has no effective-date, delayed-effect or phase-in wording for the order as a whole (the only date inside it is the 605 continuance of the Economic Stabilization Agency to October 31, 1953, which concerns that Agency, not any batch target). It is dated 'The White House, August 14, 1953', filed August 18 and printed August 20, 1953. The OFR catalog notes on all seven targets read 'Superseded by: EO 10480, August 14, 1953'. A later Federal Register Defense Mobilization Order (VII-9, printed in the file for EO 10610) cites the order as 'Executive Order 10480 of August 15, 1953'; the official text of the order itself and the OFR notes both say August 14, so 1953-08-14 is used. The project takes an order with no effective wording to be effective on signing, so every sec. 607 supersession is dated 1953-08-14.
conclusion: EO 10480 (signed 1953-08-14, 18 FR 4939-4944; the held file is the whole 44-page issue, of which the order occupies PDF pages 1 and 3-6 and was read once in full) is a successor delegation order for the Defense Production Act of 1950: Part I puts all mobilization under the Director of the Office of Defense Mobilization (ODM) and creates the Defense Mobilization Board, Part II delegates Title I priorities and allocations, Part III re-delegates the Title III expansion-of-capacity functions, Part IV is labor supply, Part V voluntary agreements, and Part VI holds definitions (sec. 601), general redelegation power (602), the abolition of the Defense Materials Procurement Agency (604), a continuance of the Economic Stabilization Agency to October 31, 1953 for liquidation (605), a continuation-of-actions clause (606), the supersession list (607) and a conflict clause (608). Sec. 607 supersedes or revokes thirteen orders in one list without qualification; all seven batch targets are in it, none is excepted, and the order states no effective date, so each supersession took effect on signing, 1953-08-14. Sec. 606 is the one savings clause: orders, regulations, rulings, certificates, directives and other actions relating to any function affected by the order stay in effect unless inconsistent, and nothing affects the validity of anything done under previous delegations under the DPA. It preserves actions taken under the superseded delegations; it does not save the superseded orders themselves, because sec. 607 expressly supersedes them (inconsistent by definition). The order re-delegates the substance of six of the seven targets (the DPA delegation orders EO 10324, 10359, 10373, 10390, 10433 and 10467), which is why those six are read as transferred_or_accrued; EO 10169 (an advisory committee that advised the National Security Resources Board under no DPA delegation) is not carried forward by any provision and is read as having no residual. Sec. 605 continues the Agency, not any batch target.
